title: The Chow test: did the coefficients change at a known date?
concepts: F statistic from residual sums of squares

explain.prompt: In 5–7 sentences: state the null hypothesis of the Chow test and how the F statistic is built; interpret the result at 2016-01-01 and at the two placebo dates; then explain why the same test on log *levels* rejects even at a placebo date, and why that result must be ignored. What assumptions does the Chow test need, and which ones guided your choice of regression?
rubric: H0: the regression coefficients (constant and slope) are identical before and after the known date; H1: at least one differs.

F = [(SSR_pooled − SSR_1 − SSR_2)/k] / [(SSR_1 + SSR_2)/(n − 2k)] with k = 2: how much the fit improves when each period gets its own line, relative to the remaining noise; compared with an F(k, n − 2k) distribution.

At 2016-01-01 on daily log returns: F ≈ 107, p ≈ 0 → the short-run relationship changed (pass-through ≈ 0.59 → 0.89). Placebo dates inside a regime: p ≈ 0.92 (2018) and ≈ 0.50 (2014) → no change, as expected.

On log levels the test rejects even at the 2018 placebo (F ≈ 67): the variables are I(1) and the residuals are highly persistent, so the F distribution does not apply — the rejection is an artefact, like the spurious t-stats of Case 2.

Assumptions: date known in advance; stationary variables; errors independent over time with the same variance in both sub-periods. Daily log returns satisfy them far better than levels — hence the regression on returns.
Chow tests parameter equality; it does not locate an unknown break and says nothing about why the change happened — the economic mechanism (end of the export ban) does.
